reader.title: False report of the lynching of J. J. Bowles
bases: A widely reprinted report that cowboys hanged J. J. Bowles near Fort Maginnis proved false: Bowles was seen travelling, wrote denying it, and the River Press admitted its error (A12, A14, A17); no paper gives his race (A2, A4).

The original reports described cowboys pursuing and hanging Bowles for starting a prairie fire (A2, A4), but Bowles was alive in October, denied the story himself, and the paper that started it retracted it (A12, A14, A17), so no one was killed.
The hanging was reported by the River Press and Helena papers (A2, A4) and then denied by the Benton Record, by Bowles's own card and by the River Press itself (A6, A12, A17).

summary.text: The false report of the lynching of J. J. Bowles was a story, printed in Montana Territory newspapers in September 1882, that cowboys had hanged Bowles, a Judith Basin saloon keeper, near Fort Maginnis for setting a prairie fire.
The story was reprinted as far away as Omaha, Cheyenne and Savannah before Bowles himself wrote in October that it was a lie.
The Fort Benton River Press, which first published it, admitted in November that it had been wrong.
Bowles was described as an old-timer in the territory and a partner of Major Reed in a trading post and saloon near Fort Maginnis.
The Helena Independent called him "a hard case on general principles" and said he had helped capture Pelkey, the killer of Charles Tacke, in 1880.
No report gives his race.

According to the River Press of September 20, as quoted by the Helena Weekly Herald, Bowles was driving to Billings to hire girls to dance at his dive when, by accident or design, he started a prairie fire.
Cowboys working for the Stock Association were said to have asked him to help fight it, and he was said to have refused and driven on.
After putting out the fire, the cowboys reportedly followed him, caught up with him and hanged him some miles beyond Fort Maginnis.
The River Press named its source as a Mr. McGinn, just arrived from Fort Maginnis, who had the particulars from a Mr. McNamara of Broadwater, McCulloh & Co.

Doubts appeared within days: the Rocky Mountain Husbandman wrote that people from Fort Maginnis said the hanging was only rumored there, and the Benton Record said travelers had heard no such news and placed Bowles near Billings.
The River Press still quoted the Independent on October 4 that a man from the area called the hanging a fact, or at least so reported.
On October 12 the Benton Record reported that George H. Farmer had travelled ten or twelve miles with Bowles and left him at Deer Creek.
The same issue printed a card from Bowles, dated October 7 at Carruthers' ranch, calling the story "a d——d lie" and promising to prove it "to the sorrow of the Press fool."
The Butte Semi-Weekly Miner then reported him in Benton "alive and well," and the Bismarck Tribune summarized his letter.

On November 15 the River Press wrote that it had "got off wrong in bad shape" and reported that Bowles had been shot in the side by the mistress of a house at Johnny Carothers' on Arrow Creek when he tried to force his way in.
The Helena Weekly Herald ran the story under "LYNCHED" and called Bowles a "desperate man," adding that his end, "though not according to written law," would serve as a warning to desperadoes.
Papers outside Montana reprinted the Montana versions under heads such as "Lynched by Cowboys" and "A Hard Character Hung by Cowboys."
In Dakota the Mandan Times, quoted by the Jamestown Weekly Alert, renamed him "Jim Bowles" and had cowboys and settlers hang him "to the nearest cedar" in "that land of the Unwritten law."
The Rocky Mountain Husbandman took a different line, saying that a hanging on circumstantial evidence would have been unjustifiable.
The Benton Record, a local rival of the River Press, used the episode against it, calling the Helena papers that copied the story "noodle-headed locals."
The River Press first defended printing the report on the word of a credible gentleman and later retracted it.
The Helena Weekly Herald reprinted that retraction under the heading "Right This Time."

accounts.label: River Press (Sept. 20), via McGinn and McNamara
accounts.gist: Bowles started a prairie fire on the way to Billings, refused to help Stock Association cowboys fight it, and was pursued and hanged by a band they organized.

accounts.label: Helena Independent
accounts.gist: Cowboys who put out a fire Bowles had set followed him and hanged him a few miles from Fort Maginnis; later said a man from the area called the hanging a fact.

accounts.label: Mandan Times
accounts.gist: 'Jim Bowles' set a destructive forest fire and cowboys and settlers hanged him to the nearest cedar.

accounts.label: Benton Record and Bowles himself
accounts.gist: No such news reached Maginnis; Farmer travelled with Bowles, and Bowles wrote that the story was 'a d——d lie.'

framing.detail: The Helena Weekly Herald, under 'LYNCHED,' called Bowles a 'desperate man' and said his end 'will bear good fruit' as a warning to desperadoes.
The Rocky Mountain Husbandman doubted the story and said a hanging on circumstantial evidence was unjustifiable.
Papers in Billings, Omaha, Cheyenne and Savannah reprinted the Montana versions as 'Lynched by Cowboys' and 'A Hard Character Hung by Cowboys.'
The Benton Record, the River Press's local rival, called the story baseless and mocked the 'noodle-headed locals' who copied it.

conflicts.note: Bowles's own card, a named traveller's account and the River Press retraction outweigh the secondhand rumor.
Both are versions of a report that proved false.

record_check.record: River Press relays an alleged lynching; no place, date, mob or race given
record_check.dossier: The reports give a place (a few miles from Fort Maginnis), a rough date (mid-September 1882) and Stock Association cowboys; the story was then disproved

info: Alleged hanging said to have occurred Tuesday or Wednesday of the week before Sept. 28, 1882 (about Sept. 12-13); first printed by the River Press on Sept. 20

J. J. (John J.) Bowles of the Judith Basin, partner of Major Reed in a trading post and saloon near Fort Maginnis; race not stated; alive
Reported to have set a prairie fire, by accident or design, and refused to help cowboys put it out
Alleged: cowboys working for the Stock Association; the Mandan Times said cowboys and settlers
